claim: Plasmodium vivax relapse infections occur following activation of latent liver-stage parasites (hypnozoites) causing new blood-stage infections weeks to months after the initial infection.
source: Plasmodium vivax relapse infections occur following activation of latent liver-stages parasites (hypnozoites) causing new blood-stage infections weeks to months after the initial infection.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about P. vivax biology that is established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The hypnozoite reservoir is predicted to be over-dispersed with many individuals having few or no hypnozoites, and some having intensely infected livers.
source: The hypnozoite reservoir is predicted to be over-dispersed with many individuals having few or no hypnozoites, and some having intensely infected livers.
evidence: This prediction is based on the mathematical model developed in the manuscript and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Individuals with more hypnozoites are predicted to experience more relapses and contribute more to onwards P. vivax transmission.
source: Individuals with more hypnozoites are predicted to experience more relapses and contribute more to onwards P. vivax transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the model structure where more hypnozoites lead to more activation events, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Incorporating hypnozoite killing drugs such as primaquine into first-line treatment regimens is predicted to cause substantial reductions in P. vivax transmission as individuals with the most hypnozoites are more likely to relapse and be targeted for treatment.
source: Incorporating hypnozoite killing drugs such as primaquine into first-line treatment regimens is predicted to cause substantial reductions in P. vivax transmission as individuals with the most hypnozoites are more likely to relapse and be targeted for treatment.
evidence: This prediction is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 5C and Figure 6.

claim: P. vivax is the geographically most widely distributed species of malaria in the world, causing in the region of 80–300 million clinical episodes every year.
source: This is in spite of P. vivax being the geographically most widely distributed species of malaria in the world, causing in the region of 80–300 million clinical episodes every year (Mueller et al., 2009a; Gething et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mueller et al., 2009a and Gething et al., 2012.

claim: P. falciparum models are not applicable to P. vivax as they fail to account for the reservoir of dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) which give rise to relapsing infections.
source: P. falciparum models are not applicable to P. vivax as they fail to account for the reservoir of dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) which give rise to relapsing infections—one of the defining characteristics of the biology and epidemiology of P. vivax (Mueller et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the biological differences between P. falciparum and P. vivax, supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2009a.

claim: When a P. vivax infected mosquito takes a blood meal from a human, sporozoites are injected into the skin and migrate to the liver, where they invade hepatocytes and develop into either actively dividing schizonts or dormant hypnozoites.
source: When a P. vivax infected mosquito takes a blood meal from a human, sporozoites are injected into the skin and migrate to the liver, where they invade hepatocytes and develop into either actively dividing schizonts or dormant hypnozoites.
evidence: This describes the established life cycle of P. vivax parasites.

claim: The development of actively dividing schizonts may lead to a primary blood-stage infection and potentially clinical malaria.
source: The development of actively dividing schizonts may lead to a primary blood-stage infection and potentially clinical malaria (Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2013.

claim: Hypnozoites will lie dormant in the liver for weeks to years before activating to initiate new blood-stage infections.
source: Hypnozoites will lie dormant in the liver for weeks to years before activating to initiate new blood-stage infections.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hypnozoite behavior.

claim: The biological mechanisms regulating the activation of hypnozoites remain unknown.
source: The biological mechanisms regulating the activation of hypnozoites remain unknown (Mueller et al., 2009a), although a number of triggers for relapses have been proposed, including fever caused by other pathogens such as P. falciparum (Shanks and White, 2013) and exposure to Anopheles-specific proteins (Hulden and Hulden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2009a and represents current scientific understanding.

claim: Fever caused by other pathogens such as P. falciparum has been proposed as a trigger for relapses.
source: The biological mechanisms regulating the activation of hypnozoites remain unknown (Mueller et al., 2009a), although a number of triggers for relapses have been proposed, including fever caused by other pathogens such as P. falciparum (Shanks and White, 2013) and exposure to Anopheles-specific proteins (Hulden and Hulden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shanks and White, 2013.

claim: Exposure to Anopheles-specific proteins has been proposed as a trigger for relapses.
source: The biological mechanisms regulating the activation of hypnozoites remain unknown (Mueller et al., 2009a), although a number of triggers for relapses have been proposed, including fever caused by other pathogens such as P. falciparum (Shanks and White, 2013) and exposure to Anopheles-specific proteins (Hulden and Hulden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hulden and Hulden, 2011.

claim: Strains from tropical areas have an average time to first relapse of 3–6 weeks.
source: There is considerable geographical variation in the timing and frequency of P. vivax relapse infections, with strains from tropical areas having an average time to first relapse of 3–6 weeks and long-latency strains from temperate areas relapsing within 6–9 months (Lover and Coker, 2013; Battle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lover and Coker, 2013 and Battle et al., 2014.

claim: Long-latency strains from temperate areas relapse within 6–9 months.
source: There is considerable geographical variation in the timing and frequency of P. vivax relapse infections, with strains from tropical areas having an average time to first relapse of 3–6 weeks and long-latency strains from temperate areas relapsing within 6–9 months (Lover and Coker, 2013; Battle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lover and Coker, 2013 and Battle et al., 2014.

claim: Following a single infection with a tropical strain of P. vivax the time until next relapse has been observed to increase with each successive relapse.
source: For example, following a single infection with a tropical strain of P. vivax the time until next relapse has been observed to increase with each successive relapse (Berliner et al., 1948; White, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berliner et al., 1948 and White, 2011.

claim: Temperate strains are associated with a long latency period until first relapse (of the order of 6 months) followed by short intervals between successive relapses.
source: In contrast, temperate strains are associated with a long latency period until first relapse (of the order of 6 months) followed by short intervals between successive relapses (Coatney et al., 1950; Hankey et al., 1953; White, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coatney et al., 1950, Hankey et al., 1953, and White, 2011.

claim: In each ecological zone, the number of hypnozoites N and the hypnozoite activation rate α were correlated.
source: In each ecological zone, the number of hypnozoites N and the hypnozoite activation rate α were correlated (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model fitting results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A short time to relapse could be explained by a single fast activating hypnozoite or a large number of slow activating hypnozoites.
source: For example, a short time to relapse could be explained by a single fast activating hypnozoite or a large number of slow activating hypnozoites.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between N and α observed in the model fitting.

claim: The within-host model predicts notable dose-dependency with increased numbers of hypnozoites associated with a greater number of relapses and shorter time to first relapse.
source: This model predicts notable dose-dependency with increased numbers of hypnozoites associated with a greater number of relapses and shorter time to first relapse.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 showing sample relapse patterns.

claim: Following the long latency to first relapse in temperate strains, the interval between subsequent relapses is considerably shorter.
source: Following the long latency to first relapse in temperate strains, the interval between subsequent relapses is considerably shorter.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 for temperate strain simulations.

claim: The within-host model assumes that hypnozoites act independently of each other, and hence the time to next relapsing hypnozoite is exponentially distributed.
source: The within-host model assumes that hypnozoites act independently of each other, and hence the time to next relapsing hypnozoite is exponentially distributed.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the mathematical model described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: If the simulated data are censored such that relapses occurring within 14 days of a previous relapse remain undetected then there is an apparent periodicity in detected relapses.
source: If the simulated data are censored such that relapses occurring within 14 days of a previous relapse remain undetected (due to either prophylaxis by blood-stage anti-malarials or the presence of parasites from an existing infection) then there is an apparent periodicity in detected relapses.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The periodicity in detected relapses is most evident for large numbers of hypnozoites with the period being determined by the assumed duration of prophylactic protection.
source: The periodicity in detected relapses is most evident for large numbers of hypnozoites with the period being determined by the assumed duration of prophylactic protection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Periodicity in relapses could be attributable to a cycle of fevers initiating hypnozoite activation which in turn cause new blood-stage infections and malaria-associated fevers.
source: However, as has been previously argued, periodicity in relapses could also be attributable to a cycle of fevers initiating hypnozoite activation which in turn cause new blood-stage infections and malaria-associated fevers (White, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White, 2011.

claim: For tropical strains the mean number of hypnozoites in the liver is expected to decrease exponentially.
source: For tropical strains the mean number of hypnozoites in the liver is expected to decrease exponentially, but the proportion of individuals carrying hypnozoites is expected to decrease at a slower rate as an individual can relapse even if they have just one hypnozoite (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The proportion of individuals carrying hypnozoites is expected to decrease at a slower rate than the mean number of hypnozoites as an individual can relapse even if they have just one hypnozoite.
source: For tropical strains the mean number of hypnozoites in the liver is expected to decrease exponentially, but the proportion of individuals carrying hypnozoites is expected to decrease at a slower rate as an individual can relapse even if they have just one hypnozoite (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and is a logical inference from the model structure.

claim: For temperate strains the mean number of hypnozoites in the liver decreases slowly, as hypnozoites remain in the long-latency phase for approximately 6 months.
source: For temperate strains the mean number of hypnozoites in the liver decreases slowly, as hypnozoites remain in the long-latency phase for approximately 6 months (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The expected number of relapsing hypnozoites per individual is expected to follow an approximately exponential distribution.
source: The expected number of relapsing hypnozoites per individual is expected to follow an approximately exponential distribution (Figure 3E,F) in agreement with empirical observations (Horing, 1947; White, 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E,F and supported by citations to Horing, 1947 and White, 2011.

claim: The proportion of people infected with hypnozoites is predicted to be higher than the proportion infected with P. vivax blood-stage parasites.
source: The proportion of people infected with hypnozoites is predicted to be higher than the proportion infected with P. vivax blood-stage parasites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For a given EIR, P. vivax blood-stage prevalence is predicted to be higher than P. falciparum prevalence as a single mosquito bite can give rise to multiple blood-stage infections.
source: For a given EIR, P. vivax blood-stage prevalence is predicted to be higher than P. falciparum prevalence as a single mosquito bite can give rise to multiple blood-stage infections.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and is an inference from the model structure.

claim: The median number of hypnozoites increases with increasing P. vivax transmission.
source: Figure 4B shows how the median number of hypnozoites increases with increasing P. vivax transmission.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The number of hypnozoites per individual is predicted to follow a negative binomial distribution.
source: The number of hypnozoites per individual is predicted to be over-dispersed following a negative binomial distribution.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and is an inference from the model structure.

claim: The introduction of vector control is expected to cause a rapid decline in P. falciparum parasite rate (PfPR), and a smaller and slower decline in P. vivax.
source: The introduction of vector control is expected to cause a rapid decline in P. falciparum parasite rate (PfPR), and a smaller and slower decline in P. vivax (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing treatment coverage with blood-stage anti-malarials leads to reductions in blood-stage prevalence of both P. falciparum and P. vivax.
source: Increasing treatment coverage leads to reductions in blood-stage prevalence of both P. falciparum and P. vivax.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The reduction in the P. vivax hypnozoite rate is slow when using blood-stage anti-malarials alone as the hypnozoite reservoir is not directly targeted.
source: Notably the reduction in the P. vivax hypnozoite rate is slow as the hypnozoite reservoir is not directly targeted.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and is an inference from the model structure.

claim: The inclusion of primaquine in first-line treatment regimens is predicted to cause substantial reductions in both the P. vivax parasite rate and hypnozoite rate.
source: The inclusion of primaquine in first-line treatment regimens is predicted to cause substantial reductions in both the P. vivax parasite rate and hypnozoite rate (Figure 5C), as individuals being treated for blood-stage P. vivax infections will also have their hypnozoites removed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Individuals with the most hypnozoites are most likely to relapse and potentially be detected by health systems.
source: A consequence of this strategy is that the hypnozoite reservoir can be targeted efficiently, as individuals with the most hypnozoites are most likely to relapse and potentially be detected by health systems.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model structure and is demonstrated in Figure 6.

claim: The inclusion of primaquine in first-line treatment regimens preferentially targets the most intense infections, with the greatest reductions observed in individuals with the most hypnozoites.
source: Figure 6 shows how the inclusion of primaquine in first-line treatment regimens preferentially targets the most intense infections, with the greatest reductions observed in individuals with the most hypnozoites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hypnozoites in the liver constitute a third malaria parasite reservoir, in addition to the reservoirs in the blood circulation and mosquito also present for P. falciparum.
source: Hypnozoites in the liver constitute a third malaria parasite reservoir, in addition to the reservoirs in the blood circulation and mosquito also present for P. falciparum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the differences between P. vivax and P. falciparum.

claim: Hypnozoites are assumed to be subjected to two processes: activation at constant rate α, and death at constant rate µ.
source: Hypnozoites are assumed to be subjected to two processes: activation at constant rate α, and death at constant rate µ.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the mathematical model.

claim: By considering infection with batches of hypnozoites, simple processes of constant activation and death can explain many of the complex patterns observed in P. vivax relapses.
source: By considering infection with batches of hypnozoites, these simple processes can explain many of the complex patterns observed in P. vivax relapses (see Box 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A key assumption in the proposed model is the constant activation of hypnozoites.
source: A key assumption in the proposed model is the constant activation of hypnozoites.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption.

claim: The constant activation assumption implies that relapses can occur immediately after primary P. vivax infection.
source: This implies that relapses can occur immediately after primary P. vivax infection, in contrast to suggestions that the first relapse does not occur until 2–3 weeks later.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the constant activation assumption.

claim: Except in cases with documented chloroquine resistance, recurrent infections are rarely observed prior to day 14 in treatment efficacy studies.
source: Except in cases with documented chloroquine resistance (Price et al., 2014), recurrent infections are rarely observed prior to day 14, however the inclusion of long-lasting anti-malarials in treatment regimens provides prophylaxis during this period making detection of parasites unlikely.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Price et al., 2014.

claim: In a recent study of dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP), Tarning et al. (2014) tested a model where relapses occur in bursts every 3 weeks, but it arguably provided no better fit to the data than a model of constant hypnozoite activation.
source: In a recent study of the slowly eliminated drug dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP) Tarning et al. (2014) tested a model where relapses occur in bursts every 3 weeks, but it arguably provided no better fit to the data than a model of constant hypnozoite activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tarning et al., 2014.

claim: The model does not account for the potential role of triggers of hypnozoite activation such as febrile illness.
source: The potential role of triggers of hypnozoite activation such as febrile illness (Shanks and White, 2013) are not accounted for.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: There is no heterogeneity or seasonality in transmission, and no age structure in the model.
source: There is no heterogeneity or seasonality in transmission, and no age structure.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: Incorporation of the acquisition of natural immunity into the model will be particularly important for settings with high transmission intensity where immunity has a role in regulating blood-stage infections.
source: Incorporation of the acquisition of natural immunity into the model will be particularly important for settings with high transmission intensity where immunity has a role in regulating blood-stage infections (Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2013 and represents a limitation of the current model.

claim: It is assumed that all individuals infected with blood-stage parasites are capable of transmitting to mosquitoes.
source: It is assumed that all individuals infected with blood-stage parasites are capable of transmitting to mosquitoes.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption.

claim: P. falciparum and P. vivax parasite prevalence (PfPR and PvPR) are the most widely reported and best validated metrics of malaria transmission from epidemiological studies.
source: P. falciparum and P. vivax parasite prevalence (PfPR and PvPR) are the most widely reported and best validated metrics of malaria transmission from epidemiological studies (Gething et al., 2011a; Gething et al., 2012) providing measurements of the proportion of individuals with detectable blood-stage parasites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gething et al., 2011a and Gething et al., 2012.

claim: In settings with similar levels of P. vivax and P. falciparum transmission, the model predicts PvPR to be greater than PfPR due to the additional blood-stage infections arising from relapses.
source: In settings with similar levels of P. vivax and P. falciparum transmission, the model predicts PvPR to be greater than PfPR due to the additional blood-stage infections arising from relapses.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Empirical observations find PfPR to be similar to or greater than PvPR.
source: However, this does not agree with empirical observations which find PfPR to be similar to or greater than PvPR (Snounou and White, 2004; Mueller et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Snounou and White, 2004 and Mueller et al., 2009b.

claim: The discrepancy between model predictions and empirical observations is most likely explained by the rapid acquisition of immunity to P. vivax, the low detectability of P. vivax blood-stage infections, and the longer durations of P. falciparum blood-stage infection not captured in the model.
source: This is most likely explained by the rapid acquisition of immunity to P. vivax (Koepfli et al., 2013; Mueller et al., 2013) the low detectability of P. vivax blood-stage infections (Harris et al., 2010), and the longer durations of P. falciparum blood-stage infection (Molineaux et al., 2001) not captured in the model.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koepfli et al., 2013, Mueller et al., 2013, Harris et al., 2010, and Molineaux et al., 2001.

claim: The additional P. vivax parasite reservoir in the liver means that PfPR and PvPR are not directly comparable metrics.
source: Furthermore, the additional P. vivax parasite reservoir in the liver means that PfPR and PvPR are not directly comparable metrics.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the biological differences between P. vivax and P. falciparum.

claim: If a parasitological survey indicates similar parasite prevalence, a greater control effort will be required to reduce P. vivax transmission than to reduce P. falciparum transmission because of the additional infections emerging from the hypnozoite reservoir.
source: Thus if a parasitological survey indicates similar parasite prevalence, a greater control effort will be required to reduce P. vivax transmission than to reduce P. falciparum transmission because of the additional infections emerging from the hypnozoite reservoir.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model structure and the presence of the hypnozoite reservoir.

claim: Vector control interventions that increase mosquito mortality are expected to cause greater reductions in PfPR than PvPR, as higher levels of P. vivax transmission can be maintained with fewer mosquito bites.
source: Vector control interventions that increase mosquito mortality are expected to cause greater reductions in PfPR than PvPR (Figure 5A), as higher levels of P. vivax transmission can be maintained with fewer mosquito bites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and is an inference from the model structure.

claim: Increased vector control has caused greater reductions in P. falciparum than P. vivax in both Thailand and Brazil.
source: This has been observed in both Thailand (Sattabongkot et al., 2004) and Brazil (Coura et al., 2006) where increased vector control has caused greater reductions in P. falciparum than P. vivax.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sattabongkot et al., 2004 and Coura et al., 2006.

claim: In P. vivax and P. falciparum co-endemic regions, heterogeneity in exposure to mosquito bites may cause associations between P. falciparum fevers and the risk of future P. vivax relapses.
source: In P. vivax and P. falciparum co-endemic regions, heterogeneity in exposure to mosquito bites may cause associations between P. falciparum fevers and the risk of future P. vivax relapses (Douglas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Douglas et al., 2011.

claim: The inclusion of primaquine in first-line treatment for P. falciparum may also reduce P. vivax transmission.
source: Thus the inclusion of primaquine in first-line treatment for P. falciparum may also reduce P. vivax transmission.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the association between P. falciparum and P. vivax infections.

claim: In treatment-reinfection studies of Papua New Guinean children, mass administration of drugs such as chloroquine or artemether-lumefantrine successfully cleared P. vivax blood-stage infections but rapid recurrence of infection was observed during follow-up—most likely due to relapses.
source: In treatment-reinfection studies of Papua New Guinean children (Betuela et al., 2012; Robinson et al., unpublished), mass administration of drugs such as chloroquine or artemether-lumefantrine successfully cleared P. vivax blood-stage infections but rapid recurrence of infection was observed during follow-up—most likely due to relapses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Betuela et al., 2012 and Robinson et al., unpublished.

claim: The addition of primaquine to the treatment regimen caused large reductions in the rate of recurrent infections in Papua New Guinean children.
source: The addition of primaquine to the treatment regimen caused large reductions in the rate of recurrent infections.
evidence: This is supported by the citation to studies in Papua New Guinean children.

claim: Primaquine treatment clears the hypnozoite reservoir but requires a difficult 14 day treatment regimen.
source: Although primaquine treatment clears the hypnozoite reservoir, it requires a difficult 14 day treatment regimen, and is not without risk due to vulnerability to haemolytic toxicity among glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficient patients (Howes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about primaquine treatment, supported by citation to Howes et al., 2013.

claim: Primaquine is not without risk due to vulnerability to haemolytic toxicity among glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficient patients.
source: Although primaquine treatment clears the hypnozoite reservoir, it requires a difficult 14 day treatment regimen, and is not without risk due to vulnerability to haemolytic toxicity among glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficient patients (Howes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Howes et al., 2013.

claim: Individuals should be tested for G6PD deficiency before the administration of primaquine.
source: Individuals should thus be tested for G6PD deficiency (Kim et al., 2011) before the administration of primaquine.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011.

claim: Tafenoquine is currently undergoing phase three trials and is likely to be licensed for use by 2017.
source: A primaquine analogue, tafenoquine, is currently undergoing phase three trials and is likely to be licensed for use by 2017 (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2014.

claim: Tafenoquine requires a single dose alongside a 3 day chloroquine regimen.
source: Tafenoquine requires a single dose alongside a 3 day chloroquine regimen, but is subject to the same risks in G6PD deficient patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tafenoquine treatment.

claim: Tafenoquine is subject to the same risks in G6PD deficient patients as primaquine.
source: Tafenoquine requires a single dose alongside a 3 day chloroquine regimen, but is subject to the same risks in G6PD deficient patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tafenoquine treatment.

claim: In the absence of effective diagnostics for detecting liver-stage parasites, models will play a crucial role in estimating and predicting the effectiveness of interventions that target the hypnozoite reservoir.
source: In the absence of effective diagnostics for detecting liver-stage parasites (malERA Consultative Group on Diagnoses and Diagnostics, 2011), models will play a crucial role in estimating and predicting the effectiveness of interventions that target the hypnozoite reservoir, either indirectly via vector control and blood-stage anti-malarials or directly via primaquine treatment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to malERA Consultative Group on Diagnoses and Diagnostics, 2011 and is a logical inference about the role of models.

claim: The number of hypnozoites following a primary infection is assumed to be geometrically distributed.
source: Based on evidence that the number of sporozoites injected with a mosquito bite approximately follows a geometric distribution (Beier et al., 1991), we assume that the number of hypnozoites following a primary infection is also geometrically distributed.
evidence: This is a model assumption based on citation to Beier et al., 1991.

claim: The number of sporozoites injected with a mosquito bite approximately follows a geometric distribution.
source: Based on evidence that the number of sporozoites injected with a mosquito bite approximately follows a geometric distribution (Beier et al., 1991), we assume that the number of hypnozoites following a primary infection is also geometrically distributed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beier et al., 1991.

claim: Each hypnozoite acts independently of other hypnozoites.
source: Underlying assumptions of this model are: (i) each hypnozoite acts independently of other hypnozoites, for example, hypnozoites will not activate in batches due to mechanisms such as quorum sensing; and, (ii) hypnozoite death occurs at a constant rate, due to either death of the hypnozoite within the hepatocyte or death of the hepatocyte itself (Malato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption.

claim: Hypnozoites will not activate in batches due to mechanisms such as quorum sensing.
source: Underlying assumptions of this model are: (i) each hypnozoite acts independently of other hypnozoites, for example, hypnozoites will not activate in batches due to mechanisms such as quorum sensing; and, (ii) hypnozoite death occurs at a constant rate, due to either death of the hypnozoite within the hepatocyte or death of the hepatocyte itself (Malato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption.

claim: Hypnozoite death occurs at a constant rate, due to either death of the hypnozoite within the hepatocyte or death of the hepatocyte itself.
source: Underlying assumptions of this model are: (i) each hypnozoite acts independently of other hypnozoites, for example, hypnozoites will not activate in batches due to mechanisms such as quorum sensing; and, (ii) hypnozoite death occurs at a constant rate, due to either death of the hypnozoite within the hepatocyte or death of the hepatocyte itself (Malato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption and supported by citation to Malato et al., 2011.

claim: The activation of a hypnozoite may not directly correspond to a detected relapse.
source: The activation of a hypnozoite may not directly correspond to a detected relapse. For example, an infection arising from two hypnozoites activating within a day of each other is likely to be classified as a single relapse.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between hypnozoite activation and detected relapses.

claim: An infection arising from two hypnozoites activating within a day of each other is likely to be classified as a single relapse.
source: For example, an infection arising from two hypnozoites activating within a day of each other is likely to be classified as a single relapse.
evidence: This is a logical inference about detection of relapses.

claim: Before a hypnozoite is capable of activating in temperate strains, it must undergo a long-latency phase of duration d.
source: We assume that before a hypnozoite is capable of activating, it must undergo a long-latency phase of duration d.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption for temperate strains.

claim: During the long-latency phase hypnozoites are subject to death at rate µ.
source: During this period hypnozoites are subject to death at rate µ.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption for temperate strains.

claim: The time spent in the temperate long-latency phase can be described by a gamma distribution with mean d and variance d2/M.
source: In particular, we assume that the time spent in the temperate long-latency phase can be described by a gamma distribution with mean d and variance d2/M.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption for temperate strains.

claim: It is assumed that all hypnozoites in an infection must undergo some waiting period before any of them can activate in temperate strains.
source: In the model implemented here, it is assumed that all hypnozoites in an infection must undergo some waiting period before any of them can activate, and that during the long-latency phase hypnozoites are at risk of death due to natural hepatocyte death.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption for temperate strains.

claim: During the long-latency phase hypnozoites are at risk of death due to natural hepatocyte death.
source: In the model implemented here, it is assumed that all hypnozoites in an infection must undergo some waiting period before any of them can activate, and that during the long-latency phase hypnozoites are at risk of death due to natural hepatocyte death.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model assumption for temperate strains.

claim: The within-host model for tropical relapses was fitted to data on time to first relapse infection from three ecological zones with tropical strains of P. vivax: South America, South East Asia and Melanesia.
source: The within-host model for tropical relapses was fitted in a Bayesian framework to data on time to first relapse infection from three ecological zones with tropical strains of P. vivax: South America, South East Asia and Melanesia (see Source data 1).
evidence: This describes the model fitting procedure.

claim: The data are described in detail by Battle et al. (2014).
source: The data are described in detail by Battle et al. (2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Battle et al., 2014.
